h1: Craft beer distribution models: direct, distributor or both
title: Craft Beer Distribution Models | Craft Beer School
desc: Compare direct sales, distributors and a hybrid for craft beer, with margins, cash timing, control and the legal limits that apply to alcohol.
teaser: Who delivers your beer? Who gets paid when? Each model puts the margin, the cash and the control somewhere different.
standfirst: Selling beer is a chain of hands. Each hand keeps a margin. This guide compares the three common models and shows how to choose with numbers.
sections:
You can sell direct to the customer, sell through a distributor or do both. Direct keeps the margin and the relationship but asks more of your time and cash. A distributor gives reach and handles logistics but takes a share and sits between you and the buyer.

Alcohol distribution is regulated. In India it is a state subject, so who may sell to whom, what pass-through is allowed and how the supply chain is licensed differ from state to state and change. In other countries similar tiers may apply. Check the rules with the regulator or a licensing adviser before you design the model.

Direct means the taproom, your own sales to bars and restaurants, events or home delivery where allowed. You get the full price and know your customer. You also carry delivery, collection of payment, returns and the cold chain. Cash comes quickly in a taproom and slowly from a restaurant that pays in 60 days.

Direct suits a brewery whose volume is small and whose customers are close. It stops working when the time you spend selling is time you should spend brewing.

A distributor buys from you or holds your stock. It sells on to retailers or bars. It keeps a margin for storage, transport, credit risk and the sales team. A good one opens doors you could not. A poor one lets your beer sit warm in a godown. Check the cold chain, because a hoppy beer left in heat will taste stale. Read beer off flavours for what that does.

Ask how they treat small brands, how fast they pay, how they handle returns and whether they will share sales data. An exclusive deal ties you to one partner, so make sure it has a performance clause and a way out.
A worked illustration of the chain

Use hypothetical numbers in currency units. A retailer sells your beer for 100 a litre. The retailer keeps 20, so the distributor receives 80 from the retailer. The distributor keeps 15, so you receive 65. Duty and taxes may sit in these figures in ways that differ by state, so build this chain from your own invoices.

Selling the same beer yourself to that retailer at 80, less your own delivery cost of say 8, would return 72. The gap of 7 per litre is what you pay the distributor for reach, credit and logistics. At 5,000 litres a month that is 35,000. Is the reach worth it? If the distributor sells three times the volume you could sell alone, yes. If it only matches your own sales, no. Selling to a consumer through your own taproom or web shop, where allowed, could return as much as 92, which is why the direct end of the range is so attractive on paper.

Most craft breweries end up with a mix: the taproom and a few local accounts direct, a distributor for other cities and online or retail partners for the rest. The danger is conflict, when your own price undercuts the distributor's. Set one price list and stick to it. Give every channel a reason to stay: the distributor gets the trade price and reach, the taproom gets the freshest beer and the full retail price. An online partner gets a clear territory. Our guide on pricing beer for retail shelves covers how.

Score each option on margin per litre, cash days, reach, control of quality and effort required. Weigh them for your stage. A first-year brewery rarely needs a national reach but needs cash. A brewery with spare capacity may value a distributor's volume most. See the taproom-only model at the direct end of the spectrum.

Whatever you choose, test it on a small area first. Run one city or one distributor for three months, track the sales and the payment days, then decide whether to widen it. Write down the terms: price, payment days, returns, territory and exit. If you want to model channels with your own numbers, the course below does that.
faqs: Is it better to sell direct or through a distributor?
Neither is better in general. Direct keeps margin and control. A distributor gives reach and handles logistics. Model both for your volume.
Can a small brewery sign an exclusive distribution deal?
It can, but the terms matter. Include performance targets, payment days and a way out.
Who is responsible for the cold chain?
Agree it in writing. Beer that is stored warm loses flavour. Customers blame the brand, not the distributor.
Are distribution rules the same everywhere?
No. They differ by country and, in India, by state. Check with the regulator or a licensing adviser.
